newsitem.title: UK: Britain, France rein in weapons during Iraq strike.
newsitem.headline: Britain, France rein in weapons during Iraq strike.

text.p: Britain and France, who enthusiastically weighed in behind Washington during the 1991 Gulf War, held back from Tuesday's cruise missile attack against Iraqi installations.
Britain loudly applauded the U.S. strikes but stopped short of adding any of its own hardware, while France has said very little at all.

Britain, France and the United States have kept a tripartite alliance in the region since the 1991 Gulf War against Iraq, patrolling no-fly zones over both the north and the south of the country in defence of Kurdish and Shi'ite Moslem minorities.
But the European contributions are minimal.

While the United States has 23,000 troops, more than 300 warplanes and 20 ships patrolling the region, Britain and France weigh in with only a few dozen aircraft, a couple of warships and several hundred troops.
About 200 British air force staff support six Tornado GR-1 reconnaissance and ground attack planes at a combined Allied base in Dhahran, in Saudi Arabia.

Britain keeps six Tornadoes and a VC-10 tanker for in-air refuelling at a NATO base at Incirlik, near Adana in Turkey. They are all equipped with laser-guided bombs, anti-armour cluster bombs and JP233 runway-busting bombs.
Britain's navy has two destroyers on patrol in the Gulf -- the York and the Exeter. They carry Sea Dart missiles, torpedoes and Lynx helicopters.

None of the British forces helped in Washington's missile assault, a defence ministry spokesman said. "Our only support was logistic support in allowing Diego Garcia (to be used) for refuelling," the spokesman said.

Diego Garcia, a tiny Indian Ocean coral atoll, is owned by Britain. But the United States keeps a naval communications centre and base there, along with a large airstrip built especially for the wide-winged B-52 bombers that delivered many of the cruise missiles.
Britain must give permission for each offensive's use of the base. B-52s were launched from the atoll during the Gulf War.
France has 40 Mirage 2000 fighter planes at Dhahran and about 134 staff associated with them, and half a dozen Jaguars and 123 staff at the NATO base at Incirlik.

Both the British and French forces take part in routine daily patrols over Iraq, watching troop movements, and helped compile evidence of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's recent moves ahead of Tuesday's attack.

And while they can now be expected to patrol the newly enlarged no-fly zone and watch to see how Saddam responds to the missile attacks against his southern air defences, they have otherwise contributed almost nothing militarily.
Paul Beaver, editor of Jane's Defence Weekly, said it was because no one wanted to gamble on being shot down over Iraq.
"I don't think anyone wanted to risk manned aircraft over Iraq at the moment," he said.
"They wouldn't be involved while the (Iraqi) air defences were still up and operating," he added, noting that the United States risked only long-range missiles in the strikes.
But he said Britain might join in any subsequent attacks.
"The Brits are fully supportive. The whole history of opposition to Saddam Hussein since 1990 shows the Brits and Americans think alike on this."

Britain was the largest contributor after the United States to the Gulf War, sending 40,000 troops and squadrons of fighter jets to the region. France sent smaller numbers but they included elite ground troops who helped cut off Saddam Hussein's army in the southern desert.

The allies generally make a strong effort to show combined contributions to any military operations. In 1993 the three countries made a joint demand, with Russian backing, that Iraq remove anti-aircraft missiles from the southern no-fly zone and a week later joined forces to bomb Iraqi targets there.
But they otherwise have kept a low profile, mostly because of Saudi sensitivities about a large Western presence.
